I mentioned this in another post and just wanted to make it more prevalent
in relation to the CL debate which I'm really tired of arguing because
everyone's (including my own) arguments are circular.

What I want to propose is the possibility that future (if they do come)
expansions to be single rarity sets or a level that's close to that (Vamps
and Library cards being distinctly different like they are is what I mean).
Does this not eliminate all argument over the game as the availability as
I've seen it has brewed down to the pro NL people stating you can make decks
out of commons? And since everything would basically be common, would this
not mean your argument is satisfied as well as the primary argument that
some rares are "inherently powerful" because there would be no rares?

Also an argument that has been posed is that Jyhad was designed as a truly
even game. If it was truly designed as a level playing field type of game,
why did they opt to not follow this line of rarity from the beginning?

Just some questions to ponder.

Vince

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Vince Johnson wrote:
>>Also an argument that has been posed is that Jyhad was designed as a truly
even game. If it was truly designed as a level playing field type of game,
why did they opt to not follow this line of rarity from the beginning?>>

Because it is a Collectible Card Game, and Rares mean more money from people
who want to get them for whatever reason. Without rarity levels, the
collectability aspect of the game is thrown out of the window, and makes some
folks mad (people are actually less inclined to buy CCGs sets that don't have
Rares, even if the Rares aren't all that good, as has been experienced with
other game releases). Even with rarity levels, there is nothing making the
particualr rares in the set all that much more useful than the commons, and in
Jyhad, they did a fine job of this in most cases. Rarity exists to make it hard
to get all the cards in a given set, so people will spend more money buying
cards, hoping to get the Rares they need to complete a set or use for decks. If
Rares are extra powerful, there is more incentive to spend lots of money to get
more rares. In Jyhad, this was not the case--there were very few "extra
powerful" rares in the set (at the time, the only chase cards were probably
Freak Drive, Pulled Fangs, and maybe Giant's Blood), thus the incentive to buy
lots and lots of cards came from needing lots of commons (which isn't an issue
in MTG. Once you have 4 of each common, you start throwing out the rest, and
being pissed that you have to pay for them to get your Time Spiral, or
whatever) and from wanting to complete sets or get cards you don't have.

As it is, there was simply no connection between the Rarity scheme and the
power of a given card. There are a lot more Rares in Jyhad on the level of Hell
Hound, Cat Burglary, and Behind You than there are on the level of Freak Drive
and Golconda. In comparison, cards like Majesty, Wake, and Theft of Vitae are
hightly potent, and much more impotant in terms of actual play value than most
Rares. Had, say, Majesty and Wake been Rare, then sure, I would buy that the
Rarity=Power balance factor was an issue. As it is, however, this was simply
not the case.

In Ancient Hearts (and noticably not in DS...), WOTC probably injected "power
rares" (which they did) in an attempt to boost lagging sales, and didn't give
any thought to the effect on game balance. They had already alientaed their
distributers on the vast over printing of the basic Jyhad set, and then
probably lost a good chunk of money on the VTES reprint debacle. When DS
finally came out, the available pool of players was limited to buy the set, and
DS suffered from being a small set with way too much stuff all over the place,
and as such, didn't have much to reccomend it (what, really, all that good came
out of DS? Thoughts Betrayed, which was a debacle in and of itself as well as
being common; Praxis Seizure cards became as good as commons; Some of the
vampires were cool. That's about it). When AH came around, they really needed
it to have a selling point. Sadly, the easiest selling point for an CCG
expansion is "power rares". Thus, ToRIII and RTI were born. Luckily, the rules
team decided that play value should take precident over sales figures (well,
whatever figures there are at this point...), and errataed all the "power
rares" to become more in line like they should be.

help in niche situations, but are they _neccesary_? I don't think so.

elimianting the contestation rules, but who wants that? Contestation was
made to create a dynamic of interaction between players, to simulate the
struggle over limited resources. The issue of uniqueness isn't solved by
limiting rares.

build good decks, and you won't do much to help players with small
collections. They have to figure out how to use commons effectively, rather
than worry about hte niche effects that rares provide to players with large

I also think that most tourney-level decks are based on commons
rather than rares - there are very few rares that I think you
can build a tourney deck around and expect it to do better than
one built around straightforward common-based strategies like
weenie bleed, weenie vote, malk stealth&bleed, ventrue vote/bleed,
those kinds of things.

As for pool-gaining cards, I think only a few of them are rares.
Minion Tap, for example, is common, as is Blood Doll. Even
Tribute to the Master is common, not rare, as someone else
pointed out already. There are a few decent rare pool-gain-type
cards (Golconda, Giant's Blood, Art Museum/etc.) but I would
say that none of them are better than the old Minion Tap/5th
Tradition standby (5th Tradition being uncommon).

This may be a bit excessive, but here's a quick summary of my
take on the Jyhad rares (no expansion set commentary right now
because that would make this even more absurdly long). (These
are organized by card type, then alphabetically, because that's
how the checklist that I was using was organized.)

-------
Cat Burglary - 1 bleed at 1 stealth. Not tourney competitive.

Distraction - cycle five cards or tap a vampire. Not tourney
competitive.

than one based on The 3rd Tradition - Progeny, but only because
you can make your Embrace deck even more weenie than your
Progeny deck. Probably not tourney-dominating, or at least I've
never heard of one winning an actual tourney.

tourney dominating.

playable. Not tourney dominating.

Magic of the Smith - get an equipment card out of your library.

version of IR Goggles. Not tourney competitive.

Psychic Projection - give +1 intercept to one minion/all minions
till your next turn. Not tourney competitive.

Psychic Veil - give +1 stealth to all vamps/all minions till
your next turn. Maybe tourney playable. Not tourney dominating.

Ritual Challenge - +1 hand damage for a Gangrel. Tourney playable.
Not tourney dominating.

Business Pressure - burn pool to gain votes. Not tourney
competitive.

Day Operation - make an action unblockable. Tourney playable.

Not tourney dominating.

Freak Drive - untap a vampire. Tourney playable. Without
repeat actions, Not tourney dominating.

Ritual of the Bitter Rose - all your vamps gain blood from one
diablerie. Not tourney competitive.

Telepathic Vote Counting - force one vamp not to vote or change
your mind about having called the vote. Maybe tourney playable.
Not tourney dominating.

Hell Hound - two-life, no bleed, no equipment ally. Not tourney
competitive.

The Knights - two life, no bleed ally. Not tourney competitive.

Political Ally - one life, three bleed ally. Maybe tourney
playable, definitely not tourney dominating.

Renegade Garou - three life, no bleed, beat-people-up ally.
Tourney playable. Not tourney dominating.

The Slashers - three life, no bleed ally. Not tourney competitive.

Thadius Zho, Mage - three life, one bleed ally. Maybe tourney
playable. Not tourney dominating.

Behind You - maneuver/dodge, usable only first round. Tourney
playable. Not tourney dominating.

Body of Sun - agg damage to you and opponent/only to opponent.
Maybe tourney playable. Not tourney dominating.

Burst of Sunlight - agg damage to you and opponent. Maybe tourney
playable. Not tourney dominating.

Conquer the Beast - weird discipline-requiring version of Trap.
Not tourney competitive.

Fists of Death - +1/+2 hand damage. Tourney playable. Not
tourney dominating. Poor man's version - Increased Strength,
no blood cost, common.

Flesh of Marble - prevent all but one damage. Tourney playable.
Not tourney dominating.

Immortal Grapple - hand strikes only for one round. Very
tourney playable. Occasionally tourney winning, but I haven't
heard of an IG deck winning a really big tourney yet - therefore
not tourney dominating. Does have a strong impact on the game
though; should have been uncommon or common rather than rare.

but not overpowered since it no longer does agg damage. Not
tourney dominating.

Aaron's Feeding Razor - hunt for two blood. Not tourney
competitive.

Ivory Bow - one ranged agg damage unique weapon. Tourney playable,
maybe. Susceptible to all the difficulties of using weapons; Not
tourney dominating.

Monocle of Clarity - ask a question, tell me no lies. Banned.

were allowed under DCI rules and original card text/binding

playable, not tourney dominating.

all Justicars - make a vamp have three votes. Tourney playable.

Not tourney competitive.

Anarch Troublemaker - tap two vampires or burn an equipment
and hand it over. May produce victory points as a max-two-minion
Misdirection, but not tourney dominating.

Arcane Library - tap to put a pool on a Tremere. Tourney playable.

dominating, mostly due to the time scale of the payoff.

Art Museum - tap to put a pool on a Toreador. Same as Arcane
Library comments.

Betrayer - burn a pool, burn another to guess the vamp and burn
the Betrayer. Tourney playable in the Legbiter-style Betrayer
deck, probably. Tourney dominating? Doubtful; it's a real nasty
deck from the looks of it but I haven't heard of it winning any
real-life major tournies.

Blood Puppy - put three of your pool on it, add more later, burn
it to gain the pool, burnable by other Methuselahs. Not tourney
competitive.

Curse of Nitocris - controller loses a pool per untap; changes
hands when the Edge does. Not tourney competitive.

Ecoterrorists - tap to put a pool on a Gangrel. Same as Arcane
Library comments.

Fragment of the Book of Nod - tap to draw two cards and discard
down. Tourney playable. Handy for card cycling but not much
better than The Barrens (common); stealable; not tourney dominating.

Giant's Blood - fill up a vamp, only usable once. Tourney playable,
but due to only one use, not tourney dominating.

Golconda: Inner Peace - a large vamp is either removed from game
to gain its capacity in pool, or its controller pays two to avoid
that. Tourney playable, but without Soul Gem tricks and no
guarantee your opponents will have big vamps to be removed, not
tourney dominating.

Hostile Takeover - everyone bids pool to buy someone's vamp.
Tourney playable. A fairly nasty card; often usable as a master-
phase bleed for about 3, although probably not if the victim
is playing a weenie deck. I seem to recall a deck using lots of
these winning a real-life tourney somewhere, but I don't think
it was Origins or anything. Probably not tourney dominating.

Kindred Society Games - victim vamp must pay a blood to untap.
Not tourney competitive.

Madness Network - Malks can act on other people's turns. Tourney
playable in the right deck. Like Betrayer, I haven't heard of
these decks dominating any big tournaments yet.

Malkavian Prank - guess pool, win prizes or lose pool. Maybe
tourney playable, not tourney dominating unless you have
reliable psychic powers.

Malkavian Time Auction - sell off something you have to the
highest bidder and the second-highest bidder. Not tourney
competitive.

Millicent Smith, Puritan Vampire Hunter - burns a blocked vamp.
Maybe tourney playable. Mostly just slows down the table a bit.
Not tourney dominating.

Smiling Jack, the Anarch - put your pool on him, other people
burn pool or vamp blood. Unique, burnable. Maybe tourney
playable, but I've never heard of him dominating a tourney.

Society of Leopold - victim burns a blood or is burned. Tourney
playable. A nasty card in the right deck (with Cryptic Mission),
but I've had a hard time even winning games with it, let alone
tourneys. Countermeasures are Sudden Reversal or Hunting Grounds,
which is pretty limited. Still probably not tourney dominating.

The Spawning Pool - tap to hurt a vamp after the first round.
Maybe tourney playable. Far from tourney dominating.

Succubus Club - trade stuff. Probably tourney playable. Probably
not tourney dominating unless everyone wants to make you win
for some reason.

Temptation of Greater Power - like Hostile Takeover, but costs 3
pool instead of 1 and requires a Justicar instead of a Ventrue.
However if the owner wins he pays full price instead of half.
Maybe tourney playable, probably not tourney dominating since
the pool cost gets harsh if you play a lot of them.

Vampiric Disease - diseased vampires lose blood. Not very
tourney competitive.

XTC-Laced Blood - victim vamp must hunt a lot. Burnable.
Not tourney competitive.

-------
Whew. That was lengthy. If you (or anyone) disagrees with
my assessments, please explain how the card can be more effectively
used than I think (or why it really sucks). By 'not tourney
competitive' what I mean is that playing with this card is unlikely
to help you win a tournament compared with other cards you could
use instead - due to high cost, minimal effect, whatever.

Josh

Assuming that you are talking about a CL for Rares only (which I believe you
are and have been), I assure you, the decks that will scare newbies out of
tournaments (if this is what you are worried about) are the ones made of all
commons. The weenie Pre bleed/Misdirection decks. The weenie Pre/KRC/vote
decks. The Malk high efficiency S+B decks. These are the decks that run people
over and kill them, and make them re-think their choice of entertainment. All
common based. A CL on Rares will do nothing to curtail these kinds of decks.

compete against them.

deck? An all Psychic Veil, all the time deck? These are not tourney dominating.
These are not scary. These do not frighten away the children. The newbies get
axed by:

A) S+B decks. All common.
B) S:CE decks. Majesty is common.
C) Weenie bleed/vote decks. All common.

Limiting Rares does not stop this effect. Card limits in general do not stop
this effect (the three above examples all do sparkilingly well under a blanket
CL, as their is so much redundancy in the neccessary cards. The decks that can
compete with them, however, do poorly under blanket CL).

>>but i'd like to pick up this idea. if ruse of rares is not required, why do
you fear a rare CL so much? it's fairer for less wealthy players and doesn't
hamper the deck building strategies of other people. why do you speak up
against it? i wanna know...>>

We speak up against it because:
A) It is a bad idea,
B) It does not accomplish what you hope it does,
C) It is completely unecessary,
D) It penalizes marginalized deck designs, making only the incredibly common,
obvious designs competetive.

In most cases, Rares simply do not dominate tournament play. I can think of a
handful of Rares that are used in large amounts in a competetive deck-IG in a
Pot Rush deck; Freak Drive in some weird multi action deck; well, I can't think
of any more.

For example, a CL on Rares would prevent me from playing my singularly
effective Rush combat deck, as it uses 12 IG and 8 Behind You. Without these
cards, the deck becomes unable to compete against common based decks, like
weenie bleed and any S:CE deck. Thus, my deck, which acts as a foil to these
powerful, common based deck designs, fails to act as a foil (because it is
unplayable), and these decks do better than they would have if my deck had been
playable.

Then, as to the 8 Behind You!s. You would honestly claim that my use of 8
Behind You!s is an unfair advantage I have because I managed to get up those 8
sucky Rares? Without them, my Nosferatu Rush deck would be not that good. On
the other hand, I could just play with the Brujah instead, replace all the
Behind You!s with common Flash, and have a deck that is pretty much as
effective, just more obvious.

>>but they say: "why should i play with my chances decreased by some amount as
opposed to other wealthier players? why should i play in a game where the
chances are not determined by skill and luck alone, but also by the resources i
am able to spend?" what do you say to those people?>>

Well, it is a Collectible Card Game, not the Glorious People's Socialist Card
Game Collective, so people who have lots of cards are always going to have some
sort of edge over people who have few. That is the gift and curse of CCGs. If
that is a huge problem, stay away from CCGs. There are plenty of great board
games that cost, say, 30 bucks US, you can play forever, and do not have this
issue at all--Star Fleet Battles. Titan. Diplomacy. Battletech. Whatever.

Or, more constructively, you can show them how to build tournament winning
decks that are built almost exclusively out of commons. Go digging through web
deck archives--there are plenty.

> I'm picking out those cards which i think are (or may become when the
right
> man composes the right deck) competitive tournament rares.
> they might be integral part of a real competitive deck, i.e. playing
> without
> these would make the deck inferior (no, and i don't mean you can
throw it
> in the bin, i just mean somewhat worse than without these cards), and
you
> would perhaps have to choose another deck strategy. with some notes
> starting with *

The thing is, you can obviously make decks that win tournaments
at least as often without using any of these cards ever. It's
not even a 55%/45% thing. It's a 50%/50% thing. If the only
change you make to a weenie presence bleed deck is switching out
two Social Charms for two Entrancements, there's no way the
Entrancement deck is more likely to win the tournament. Social
Charm is at least as good. Maybe better.

> Entrancement - +1 bleed or steal an ally. Tourney playable.
> Not tourney dominating.
> *a couple would enhance any presence bleed deck

Not the presence bleed decks that would rather (a) gain pool by
using Social Charm instead at superior, (b) bleed for more by
using Legal Manipulations instead, (c) tap people's vampires by
using Propaganda instead... I think you take the idea that
versatility is always good too far. Versatility is not always
good in Jyhad tourney decks.

> Far Mastery - steal an ally or retainer. Tourney playable. Not
> tourney dominating.
> *a couple would enhance any dominate bleed deck

Completely not accurate, in my opinion, since it is not a bleed
card and you have no assurance that anyone will be playing with
allies or retainers worth stealing with an action.

> Kine Dominance - +1 bleed/+1 stealth or steal a location. Tourney
> playable. Not tourney dominating.
> *a couple would enhance any dominate bleed deck, even more than the
above

Would enhance any dominate bleed deck that always has 2 blood to
blow on a mere +1 bleed. No good for weenie dominate decks.
The location stealing is occasionally really great and often
really useless.

> Day Operation - make an action unblockable. Tourney playable.
> Can produce victory points. But without Return to Innocence,
> Not tourney dominating.
> * a cool card for any ventrue bleed/vote deck

A cool card, sure, but its disadvantages are *real* and not
trivial. You have to take other cards out to put Day Ops in,
you know. What do you weaken to add unblockability to your deck?
What support mechanisms do you put in to make sure you can get
your vamps back out of torpor? Against a non-intercept-using
opponent, wouldn't Bonding be much better?

> Freak Drive - untap a vampire. Tourney playable. Without
> repeat actions, Not tourney dominating.
> * ditto. vote AND bleed in the same turn. just great

Cute but pricey at 1 blood and needing to have at least two
useful action types to take. Again, you take other things
out of your deck to put this in; will you still have enough
vote and bleed actions to get to 'double up' after squeezing
Freak Drives in? Will your vamps still have enough blood to
be useful to you?

> Fists of Death - +1/+2 hand damage. Tourney playable. Not
> tourney dominating. Poor man's version - Increased Strength,
> no blood cost, common.

A good card for one-big-strike Potence decks, but unless there
is some reason they can't use Undead Strength, Increased Strength
is even better since it costs no blood. The blood cost is very
significant in a combat deck - same reason many people use
Undead Strength rather than Pushing the Limit.

> Immortal Grapple - hand strikes only for one round. Very
> tourney playable. Occasionally tourney winning, but I haven't
> heard of an IG deck winning a really big tourney yet - therefore
> not tourney dominating. Does have a strong impact on the game
> though; should have been uncommon or common rather than rare.
> * a key card to counter majesty/presence bleed decks. a game winner

This is the only key rare I know of. It is good against Strike:
Combat Ends but crappy against Skin of Steel. It is far easier
to make a weenie bleed deck and win a tournament with it than it
is to make an IG combat deck and win a tournament with it, no
matter how many cards you own.

> Pulled Fangs - one damage, victim can't hunt. Tourney playable,
> but not overpowered since it no longer does agg damage. Not
> tourney dominating.
> * it's history but it used to be a very strong card before the errata.

Sure, but now it's got nothing on Disarm.

> Aaron's Feeding Razor - hunt for two blood. Not tourney

I really don't think this will go anywhere ever. It's unique.
You can make a deck based on getting a vampire to hunt for lots
of blood at once and sticking lots of Blood Dolls on him, but
there are much easier and more effective ways to build a pool
machine - ones that won't fall apart if your vamp with the
Razor gets beat up in combat.

> First Tradition: The Masquerade - skip turns or pay pool. Maybe
> tourney playable. Not tourney dominating.

I've played with this in friendly games, but I don't think it'd
get you anywhere in a tournament. Why not just call a Kine
Resources Contested instead?

> J.S. Simmons, Esq. - +1 bleed, unique. Tourney playable. A better
> version of Laptop Computer since he costs no pool, but not
> tourney dominating.
> *makes useful combo with freak drive

Uh huh. So does Laptop Computer. Not a useful enough combo,
especially given the existence of Archon Investigation and
Justicar Retribution.

> Tasha Morgan - +1 bleed, unique. Just like JS Simmons; tourney
> playable but not dominating.
>
> Anarch Troublemaker - tap two vampires or burn an equipment
> and hand it over. May produce victory points as a max-two-minion
> Misdirection, but not tourney dominating.
> * strong card. play it myself

I never have. No surprise factor once you put it in play, unlike
Misdirection. If you fail to oust, your prey gets to use it,
which is not exactly strong.

> Arcane Library - tap to put a pool on a Tremere. Tourney playable.
> Good for long-term pool gain or cheap vampires, but not tourney
> dominating, mostly due to the time scale of the payoff.

These are perfectly nice cards, but will never be broken because
they are *so slow*. Buying one of these even on your second
turn just puts you one action closer to being ousted by a
weenie bleed or vote deck.

> Art Museum - tap to put a pool on a Toreador. Same as Arcane
> Library comments.
>
> Betrayer - burn a pool, burn another to guess the vamp and burn
> the Betrayer. Tourney playable in the Legbiter-style Betrayer
> deck, probably. Tourney dominating? Doubtful; it's a real nasty
> deck from the looks of it but I haven't heard of it winning any
> real-life major tournies.
> *has its strenghts in environments where a certain type of deck is
most
> frequent

Which is to say, not in tournaments? ;-)

> Ecoterrorists - tap to put a pool on a Gangrel. Same as Arcane
> Library comments.
>
> Fragment of the Book of Nod - tap to draw two cards and discard
> down. Tourney playable. Handy for card cycling but not much
> better than The Barrens (common); stealable; not tourney dominating.
> *cool for weenies or freak drives. only bad if someone other than
your prey
> or predator steals it.

But hardly at all better than The Barrens. Also, it is unique,
thus limiting the impact of a card limit.

> Giant's Blood - fill up a vamp, only usable once. Tourney playable,
> but due to only one use, not tourney dominating.
> *inherently limited, so not target of my CL discussion
>
> Golconda: Inner Peace - a large vamp is either removed from game
> to gain its capacity in pool, or its controller pays two to avoid
> that. Tourney playable, but without Soul Gem tricks and no
> guarantee your opponents will have big vamps to be removed, not
> tourney dominating.

I really don't see how to abuse this. Minion Tap/Golconda could
be cute, but Minion Tap/5th Tradition/Minion Tap again is a much
easier way to gain the same amount of pool while keeping your
vamp in play the whole time.

> Hostile Takeover - everyone bids pool to buy someone's vamp.
> Tourney playable. A fairly nasty card; often usable as a master-
> phase bleed for about 3, although probably not if the victim
> is playing a weenie deck. I seem to recall a deck using lots of
> these winning a real-life tourney somewhere, but I don't think
> it was Origins or anything. Probably not tourney dominating.
> * potentially nasty, as you said. got 3 of them but didn't try in a
> tourney...

I've heard good things about this but haven't seen it in action.
Anyone who's been a victim of the crazy Hostile Takeover deck
care to comment?

> Madness Network - Malks can act on other people's turns. Tourney
> playable in the right deck. Like Betrayer, I haven't heard of
> these decks dominating any big tournaments yet.

Doesn't give you any extra actions by itself. Useful in concept
decks, but will never become a tourney-dominating archetype.
(When I make sweeping statements like that, I'm just giving my
thoughts on the card by the way. If I turn out to be wrong, feel
free to make me eat my words. ;-)

> Millicent Smith, Puritan Vampire Hunter - burns a blocked vamp.
> Maybe tourney playable. Mostly just slows down the table a bit.
> Not tourney dominating.

This is even less abusable than Society of Leopold. You don't
get to choose the vamp that burns. You don't even get to choose
whose vamp it will be. And it's unique. And it comes back to
burn your vamp if you get blocked.

> Smiling Jack, the Anarch - put your pool on him, other people
> burn pool or vamp blood. Unique, burnable. Maybe tourney
> playable, but I've never heard of him dominating a tourney.

Anarch Revolts are just plain better, in my experience.

> Society of Leopold - victim burns a blood or is burned. Tourney
> playable. A nasty card in the right deck (with Cryptic Mission),
> but I've had a hard time even winning games with it, let alone
> tourneys. Countermeasures are Sudden Reversal or Hunting Grounds,
> which is pretty limited. Still probably not tourney dominating.

It's really annoying (I think) to get your vamps burned so
easily by this card. But it's really hard to turn that into
a winning deck, because you can't do much else besides burn
vamps, and you bleed pitifully, and can't bleed at all if your
prey would torporize your vamps if you did.

> The Spawning Pool - tap to hurt a vamp after the first round.
> Maybe tourney playable. Far from tourney dominating.

This card is so far from broken, the light from broken would
take a million years to reach it. Let's see, I'm playing the
Nosferatu and I like fighting and spending blood for it. I
can either play Pushing the Limit and stuff like that, or I can
put 1 blood from a vamp on this card each turn, and then if I
block a bleed *and* press to the second round, I can use this to
do damage equal to the blood on this card to my opponent. Yeah,
that'll be effective.

> Temptation of Greater Power - like Hostile Takeover, but costs 3
> pool instead of 1 and requires a Justicar instead of a Ventrue.
> However if the owner wins he pays full price instead of half.
> Maybe tourney playable, probably not tourney dominating since
> the pool cost gets harsh if you play a lot of them.

I don't think this one can really be broken like Hostile Takeover
might be breakable. Three pool per play (as opposed to 1 for
HT) is just too much.

Josh

Messages.Author: Patrick Harris
Messages.Body:
> this is exactly my opinion. why should we limit this allowance to few
> individuals who have these cases? (well, i opened 1 case of jyhad, and have
> another one lying around waiting for sale...)

I think one problem this discussion is running into is that you seem to be
lumping "skilled player" with "big spender". An idiot with 40 cases isn't going
to do squat in a tournament. It's the skill that's going to win the tournament,
regardless of the spending done.

This, of course, discounts the player that bought 2 decks and thinks he's
tournament ready. If you can only afford a few decks of Jyhad, then you likely
can't afford any entry or travel expenses to play in the tournaments either. So
we have to assume a certain number of cards will be purchased not only for the
player to have a tournament viable deck, but to know how to play well enough to
use it. And this certainly does not entail buying boxes upon boxes of cards.
Just enough to be able to put together a deck with a theme, and to know how most
of the card will work.

> to attract more people. to not scare them off tournament play.
> to make jyhad more popular, to have more competition in tournament play.

I don't think what you propose will have any bearing on Jyhad's popularity. It
didn't with Magic. In its early days you absolutely had to have the rare cards
to win. The guy who spent the most on cards usually won. And Magic had no
problems gaining popularity. Someone, possibly you, stated earlier in this
thread that Magic is no longer like that. Regardless of whether I believe that,
Magic is not gaining popularity like it did in its early stages. If anything
it's popularity has started to wane. I know it has in my region.

> but would it enhance your deck if you had 4 or 8 of them? thats the question i
> am discussing here. and surely once you will play against somebody who plays
> that deck just with a couple of cards more than you have, and achieve better
> results with his deck. i don't say he always wins and you always lose. maybe
> its just 60-40, or 55-45. either way i think it is unnecessary to promote such
> big shot decks.

It might. It might not. You're assuming that if a common card has a rare
version, it is better. And if it is better it will always be preferred. Even
before the errata, RtI/Day Op, a combo that I'm sure you would use as an
example, isn't always better than a simple bleed. What if your prey uses a
common deflection to send it to his prey? What if he uses tons of reductions to
reduce your bleed to nothing? You've just burned your own minion and didn't
even scratch your prey. I use this case to point out that the rare cards are
*not* always better, and are *not* always preferred over the commons.

> when most people _already_ don't use that many rare cards, ewhy not limit them
> for anybody else?

This is a strange statement. If you agree with him that people don't use that
many rare cards, then what is your point? If the limit isn't going to affect
anyone, then why have it at all? There's no point in having a rule that does
nothing.

> just in general i'd like to point out that most people can't afford to play
> with 10 rares of one type, so you would not have to assume your opponents are
> playing those. but if someone actually does, he possibly hoses you because you
> don't have the force to counter it.

It may be true that most people can't afford to play with 10 rare cards of one
type. I know I can't. But your point here isn't really valid. The same can be
said about any type of deck you ignore. Most people don't play combat decks.
If you don't plan for them, however, you will probably get hosed if you
encounter one. The same can be said about voting decks and intercept decks.
*Any* type of deck, including a deck using a lot of rare cards.

> because i think it it the best deck i can build? because i think i'll win the
> tournament with that deck? why do people generally favor one deck over the
> other?

Again, this has nothing to do with the card itself, but how your skill dictates
that you to use it or not use it. Use the example of Legal Manipulations versus
Social Charm that someone used. Sure Legal Manipulations will hurt your target
more, but *only* if it goes through. If it doesn't you've just weakened your
vampire in a failed attempt. If you'd been using Social Charm, all you did was
cycle a card.

> this is a good example. if i played a rush deck, i'd take plenty of those

> [fists of death], plus some torn signposts. the deck may perform so well that

> i'd prefer it to, say, my S/B deck. but without them, it would be inferior and
> i'd take another one. why shoulöd i play a deck in a tournament of which i
> think it is not the best i could probably build?

Now you're getting into personal preference. Those Fists of Death cost blood.
You may use a big crypt where, to you, the cost is minimal. But to someone who
prefers a smaller crypt, that cost is a major issue. None of this has anything
to do with the card being rare or not. And even if it was, an opposing player
can counter it easily with a few common prevent cards.

Rare cards just have nothing to do with whether or not a deck is the best deck
you could build. It's skill. It's knowing that your opponent has no counter.
And I don't think there's a single rare that isn't countered easily, or used as
a counter itself.

If anything, rare cards do provide diversity. Mr. Suitcase does have the
advantage in that he can come up with a larger variety of decks, but that's what
you get if you have a suitcase full of cards. He may have the tools to make a
winning deck, but again, and I feel I have to stress this, it's not the rare
cards or the numbers of cards that will win. It's the skill of the player.

Perfect example: Legbiter (sorry, my friend...or acquaintance... or hmm..
Mr.Biter. Yes, that's it.)
We know he's a skilled player. (Although he could be tricking us all.)
His infamous Malkavian OOT deck does use a good number of rare cards. But that
deck is quite delicate and can be easily spoiled. It's the skill with it that
makes it win. Take the sealed-deck contests that he's in. There you have an
equal distribution of rare cards divided amongst the players. From what I've
read, he does quite well in those games as well. Again, it's the skill that
pulls him to victory. I wonder if the same thing could be said about that
pseudonym. =)

> i disagree. see above. mr. suitcase can often (not always) top the
> effectiveness of any deck composed of common cards.

I disagree with you here. See above as well. I think just as often as not, he
cannot top the effectiveness of any deck composed of common cards.

> >>Many? I can think of one: Slave Auction. And I certainly feel that there
> are better alternatives like Blood Doll and STI.<<
>
> one is even enough. but i's add eco terrorists and similar stuff to the list.

As I stated earlier in this post, there are counters. Using Ecoterrorists as an
example:It costs 2 pool - not worth it late in the game when you don't have the
pool to spend
It could be Sudden Reversal'ed
It's a location, and can be burned a number of ways - Arika, Unnatural Disaster,
Arson, Rampage..
Brainwash your uncontrolled vampires. You can't use the card to draw blood back
off your uncontrolled vampire, which is what these types often get used for.

The point is there are many ways to deal with any card. I can't think of any
that can't be dealt with somehow.

> >>Potence combat is the one exception to not needing rares (or uncommons) to
> make an effective deck. Because if anyone uses S:CE at all, your deck will be

> severely hampered. IG is a necessity for Potence based combat.<<

> >take immortal grapple, use all all nice combat rares you wish. i know it's a
> combo based on many cards, but all combat decks face this problem.<

Even this example must be qualified. Potence combat only *needs* IG in a heavy
S:CE environment. Of course most tournaments are filled with S:CE. This just
goes to show that the rare cards in this case are used to counter the non-rare
cards. And if you played in an environment free of S:CE you wouldn't need IG
anyway.

> >>Otherwise, there is no main deck strategy that requires the use of rares.
> That includes weenie bleed, weenie vote, Presence vote, Stealth & Bleed.<<
> >just because you haven't invented one doesn't mean there is none.<

This is just nonsense. You are just trying to get under his skin here. He
obviously is referring to today's tournament environment. Other than Potence
combat, there are no main deck strategies in today's tournament environments
that require the use of rare card.

And even if that deck did exist, there would be a way to counter it. And that
counter would probably involve common cards.

> but i'd like to pick up this idea. if ruse of rares is not required, why do
> you fear a rare CL so much? it's fairer for less wealthy players and doesn't
> hamper the deck building strategies of other people.
> why do you speak up against it? i wanna know...

To throw this back at you again, if you agree that the use of rare cards is not
required, then why even introduce a card limit? Under this pretext, a card
limit would *not* help less wealthy players in any way.

But you obviously don't agree that rare cards are not required. You don't seem
to mean decks that are built around rare cards. Those decks are odd, and will
surprise people for a time. But then the deck is no longer a surprise to the
players and they stop the deck in its tracks. The decks you seem to mean are
those that contain a few rare cards in place of non-rare cards (meaning those
rare cards give them the edge they needed to win).

Do you actually think that the majority of tournaments won by decks that
contained a few rare cards, if you were to take those rare cards out and replace
them with similar non-rare cards, would lose? I just cannot believe that. Rare
cards, no matter how few or how many, do not win for you. I know you haven't
said that in as many words, but you nonetheless seem to be saying it in that a
deck with rare cards will beat the same deck without rare cards, given the same
skill of player on both sides.

> > No one is going to deny that rares aren't useful to help your deck. But
> they are by no means absolutely necessary to make a competitive deck. There
> is no other reason to seek a CL
>
> not absolutely, but as you just admitted, they are useful. they can give a
> certain edge. they make a good deck a better deck. they make a better deck a
> competitive deck. they make a competitive deck a (possibly) winning deck.

Keyword there: "can". Not "do". Some decks, yes. Some decks, no. Again, this
is all personal preference as to what type of deck you want to play.

> the requirements of expensive cards drives away people who would otherwise
> like to play in a tournament environment. but they say: "why should i play
> with my chances decreased by some amount as opposed to other wealthier
> players? why should i play in a game where the chances are
> not determined by skill and luck alone, but also by the resources i am able to
> spend?" what do you say to those people?

There is no requirement of expensive cards to play, or even be viable, in a
tournament. Why do you keep saying that? If you want to play a Malkavian OOT
deck, then sure, there is a requirement of certain cards to make it work.

Answer to Q1: They aren't. I don't know who told you that, but he is wrong.
You should sit around and watch to get some ideas and see if you like it.
Answer to Q2: Your chances are determined by skill and luck. They have nothing
to do with the resources you've spent. I don't know who told you that, but he
is wrong. You should sit around and watch to get some ideas and see if you like
it.

> i would like to see more people playing jyhad. on the last tourney i attended
> were 7 participants. that's frustrating...

That is frustrating, yes. Hell, I don't even have tournaments at all here. But
I don't think the lack of distribution or interest has anything to do with card
rarities or the lack of card limits.

> >>I could build a weenie Presence deck that would have no need for any rares
> or uncommons. Social Charms and Majesties being the meat. You might add some
> uncommon Misdirections to speed it up more, but they aren't necessary.<<
> >so you would limit yourself to one deck style. is that what we want?<

He was just using that as an example because it's viable in tournament play.
There are plenty of options for players to use if they only want to stick to
common cards. Because of the heavy bleed/S:CE decks like the one proposed
above, tournament play is limited to a few deck styles (for the most part).

Will card limits change that? No.
If all cards were common, would it change that? No.
Would a Gangrel combat deck become a winning tournament deck if there were card
limits? No.
Would intercept decks suddenly become viable as a way to get to the finals if
there were no rare cards in the tournament? No.

p.

-i wonder why i always have to name cards... isn't one enough?

-you make me glad today. you just gave me a good point.

-wanna get rid of that nasty succubus? get it with no slot cost
-in your deck that features social charm for a standard.

-(after all, 6 out of 90 cards isn't that much) and your deck
-gets better. this is exactly the situation that i am talking about

> you name it. i got the impression i have been misunderstood. i didn't
> say: rares are more powerful. whether they are or are not just doesn't
> matter. i said: there are powerful cards in all rarities. but rares
> are much harder to come by, and without a CL impossible for most
> players to obtain in numbers.

So am I correct to understand that you are saying all rarities
have equal power levels (with a few obvious exceptions like ToRIII)?

-you are perfectly correct

So, the goal is to limit Mr. Suitcase's access to large numbers
of rares? But now all of a sudden, you've limited Mr. Handbag's
access to the powerful commons that he can substitute in place
of the rares he doesn't have.

-where have i done this?????

A CL doesn't magically make it easier for people to get rares
in numbers. Look at Magic's early days. All tournaments played
with a 4CL as did many play groups. Did that make getting a Lotus
or a Mox any easier? No. It still takes a heck of a lot of cards
to get to the four of a given rare you are searching for, even
if you are Mr. Suitcase.

-i had no problem obtaining rares for my type II decks. it would
-have definitely been easier with a 2CL. and people with less cards
-would find that, too.

The whole point of the issue is people's ability to make
competitive decks. Mr. Handbag can make a deck that is just
as competitive with a box full of commons Mr. Suitcase gave
him as Mr. Suitcase can make by using his larger access to
rares. With a CL, Mr. Handbag can only use a small subset of
those commons Mr. Suitcase gave him.

-i got th eimpression that you didn't carefully read what this discussion
was all about.
-i started this to impose a CL on rare cards, not on commons. kust to make
sure
-we are not talking across each other...

Joshua Duffin wrote:

> IYou mean that tourney decks often have a lot of copies of some

Not only is it a myth, it's blatantly untrue. Using rare cards, or
even building decks around them, does not guarantee a winning deck.

you will eventually run into said counter during a tournament. It's
been my experience that decks based on a single card, rare or
otherwise, are usually fragile.

In fact, you shouldn't. If you try to put a counter for every
contigency in your deck, your deck will suck goat nuts. The
only possible exception is an intercept deck...but even that
type of deck will rarely ever have a winning record without a
secondary strategy built in.

Your deck needs to be focused to be competitive. Anything
that dilutes your deck will generally make it less effective.

> If you don't have the cards to make it work, it's obviously not
> the best deck you can build. It may be the deck you want to build,
> but too bad. That's how it works.

A CCG is the ultimate lesson in how capitalism works. If you
want X, you need to invest the resources needed to get it. If
you don't have the resources, you work to get them. If you
sit around and whine about how the government or society owes
X to you, you deserve to have to beg for your next meal.

> deck, but I don't have near enough Daring the Dawns.

me know and I'll hook you up.)

I play in tournaments because I enjoy competition. However, I prefer
to pit unusual strategies against other players, rather than use the
same tired decks everyone has seen. In fact, I never play the same
deck at two different tournaments. I view deck building as both
creative and strategic.

> If I'm inventing a new deck strategy, it is not a main one.

> _can_ be built without rares means that Mr. Handbag can make
> competitive decks.

friends) the retailers won't sell what they need to keep it on

the CCG in question largely dies out with the exception of a
small cult following.

a 2 card limit on specific cards? Raise your hands. Now take
a look at the history of Jyhad and compare it to the above

Why force limits when the game comes with natural limits? Most rares
come with their own special costs - if you play with too many, you're
just as screwed as if you played with none at all. Probably more
screwed, because if you play with NONE you don't have to worry about
working it into your deck mix.

If you ain't got the cards, don't build the deck or trade and scrounge

do better than those who don't put the resources into the game.

If you don't have the cards to build it, the deck is not the best you
can build, because you DON'T HAVE THE CARDS. If you want to build the
deck, get the cards. There are plenty of decks you can build that do
not require nine zillion Fists of Death. Rush decks typically require
an experienced player to be playing them anyway (or they lose badly),
so you don't WANT to encourage newbies to play a deck like that.

>> Right, but you are limiting what good deck builders can do because

The deck you mention above has been tested repeatedly in multiple
tournaments. It has been shown that "often" is an inaccurate
statement - the deck is good and effective, but the Rush deck itself
is not the same type of force to be reckoned with that a weenie Social

rares." You are going to need to show it being much more widespread.

Then show us one. Nobody is about to make major sweeping restrictions

>but i'd like to pick up this idea. if ruse of rares is not required, why
>do you fear a rare CL so much? it's fairer for less wealthy players
>and doesn't hamper the deck building strategies of other people.
>why do you speak up against it? i wanna know...

First, wealth has little to do with it. I haven't spent much more
than $250 total on cards and I can make an AWFUL lot of decks. $250
isn't a whole lot of money to spend - I have no sympathy for people
who want to make tournament-winning decks by spending $20 on a game.
As I said above, the people who invest the most resources (practice,
thought, and money) in ANY game will turn out to be the winners.
Jyhad does very well at limiting how much the 'money' factor plays in.

Now -- A TWO CARD LIMIT on rares?! Be sensible. A two card limit
removes the following deck types:

- any Potence combat (making one discipline totally useless)
- any of the later-expansion clans' decks (they just don't have very
many discipline cards as the Original Seven and HAVE to use their
rares)
- a number of neat tricks you can do with Gangrel become useless now
that they can't Freak Drive (making one clan even more useless than it
already was)
- any intercept decks (Eagle's Sight is vital if you want to be SURE
of hurting your prey - and the Ivory Bow and Sengir Dagger are
probably also going to have to be in)
- Big pool gain decks (2nd and 5th tradition are rare)

Ok, that's five major clumps of decks that can just plain NO LONGER be
built anymore because of a two-card limit on rares. But with the
two-card limit on rares, you also remove a number of good defenses
against:

- sneak & bleed (no Rush deck to take care of them anymore, and no
pool gain to outlast them)
- weenie bleed (with only 2 Atonements you can't be sure of getting
one out in time, and no Rush deck for them to fear)
- weenie vote (no point in playing intercept to stop all those pesky
Praxis Seizures since intercept can't fly anymore, and 2nd Tradition
and Delaying Tactics are rare)

So all you've really done with a 2-card limit is removed a number of
entertaining alternatives, and encouraged the use of three very common
deck-types ANYWAY... which just happen to be three of the types that
will frustrate new players even more so than seeing some totally
wack-ass Gangrel Freak Drive special take four actions per vampire per
turn and finally bleed for lots. =)

>> No one is going to deny that rares aren't useful to help your
>> deck. But they are by no means absolutely necessary to make
>> a competitive deck. There is no other reason to seek a CL
>
>not absolutely, but as you just admitted, they are useful.
>they can give a certain edge. they make a good deck a better deck.
>they make a better deck a competitive deck. they make a competitive deck a
>(possibly) winning deck.
>the requirements of expensive cards drives away people who would otherwise
>like to play in a tournament environment. but they say: "why should
>i play with my chances decreased by some amount as opposed to other
>wealthier players? why should i play in a game where the chances are
>not determined by skill and luck alone, but also by the resources i am
>able to spend?" what do you say to those people?

"Why are you playing any game but Monopoly, where the chances are
solely determined by luck and a minimum of skill? You certainly can't
play any OTHER game this way - resources are a primary ingredient in
any game of any significant complexity you wish to play. The people
who choose to apply the resources to the game will be better at it
than you. Rejoice that you can make a competitive deck out of common
cards and the only thing spending more money will do is increase the
options for the VARIETY of your deck - not the chances of your
winning."

>i would like to see more people playing jyhad. on the last tourney i
>attended were 7 participants. that's frustrating...

hm, you missed the 15-player tourney in Atlanta, and the 20+ player
tourney in South Carolina recently. But I know that my friends in
Atlanta make a significant effort to "evangelize" the game - to draw
others in and show how much fun it can be. Most newbies find the game
sufficiently complicated in its original form so that they don't worry
about making decks with tons of Rare cards - they just want to make a
deck that does what they EXPECT it to do.

>> I could build a weenie Presence deck that would have no need
>> for any rares or uncommons. Social Charms and Majesties being
>> the meat. You might add some uncommon Misdirections to speed
>> it up more, but they aren't necessary.
>
>so you would limit yourself to one deck style. is that what we want?

If you want to build multiple deck styles, invest the resources to
support those deck styles. With the purchase of one box of Jyhad
boosters, list price about $15 these days, you can make two or three
different styles of deck. They won't necessarily be
tournament-winners, but they'll be quite effective. Buy a second box
and you can certainly make at least ONE style of tournament-winner out
of it. It may not be loaded with style (like the Horrific Countenance
deck that won in Atlanta - a common card, by the way), but it'll be
effective. If you want to play Monopoly, play Monopoly.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Sun, 9 May 1999, Vince Johnson wrote:

> What I want to propose is the possibility that future (if they do come)
> expansions to be single rarity sets or a level that's close to that (Vamps
> and Library cards being distinctly different like they are is what I mean).
> Does this not eliminate all argument over the game as the availability as
> I've seen it has brewed down to the pro NL people stating you can make decks
> out of commons? And since everything would basically be common, would this
> not mean your argument is satisfied as well as the primary argument that
> some rares are "inherently powerful" because there would be no rares?

> Also an argument that has been posed is that Jyhad was designed as a truly
> even game. If it was truly designed as a level playing field type of game,
> why did they opt to not follow this line of rarity from the beginning?

OK Dude. There are plenty of good reasons why Jyhad has and *should*
have cards of different levels of rarity. To keep things simple, I will
discuss the Jyhad set only in my comments below

Let me start with the most obvious: Some cards are Unique. You can only
have one of them in play at a time. It makes no sense to put any more
than one or two of them in a single deck. With a card like Blood Doll,
you can easily make use of 10 of them in a single deck, but not so with
Elder Library. You do not *need* as many Unique cards as you need
non-Unique cards. To have these cards at the same level of rarity would
be a waste. In Jyhad, this rule is followed almost without exception:
All unique cards are uncommon or rare...never common. The only exception
to this is The Barrens. I presume that the main reason The Barrens is
common is that it is the perfect card top help make a poorly focussed
starter deck playable.

Now heres another consideration: Some cards are "general-use" cards,
which will be playable in just about any deck. Others, however, require
specialized decks in order to be playable. Obviously, you will need alot
more of something like Wake, usab6le in just about any deck and which you
therefore might put in multiple decks, than you will need something only
playable in some narrowly focussed Nosferatu Political deck (which the
typical player will not have more than one of at a given time). Take, for
example, Art Museum. It is a pretty good card, but that is *not* why it
is rare. It is rare because in order to make it useful, you need a
Toreador in your Active region AND in your inactive region. In order to
make maximum use of it, you have to have enough cards to construct an
all-Toreador crypt -- which practically requires that you have a full set
of vampires. A beginning player, who does not even have all the vampires
yet, simply does not need to have this card at all, much less have it in
multiples. Similarly, it is only right that KRC, which has no requirement
and can be used in any political deck, should be more common than Parity
Shift, which can only be used by one's princes, assuming one has one in
play.

The above playability factor is extremely important for enabling people to
make playable (though not necessarily competitive) decks from a limited
card supply. Different rarities is the only thing that has enabled the
Sabbat set to do so well as a stand-alone game. The Sealed Deck Sabbat
tournament format with is becoming popular, works as well as it does only
because most of the cards received are commons, which have far less
playability requirements than uncommon or rare cards. If one were to
receive equal proportions of rares and uncommons in each booster, then it
would be far more difficult to construct playable decks from just a few
boosters. This is not merely important for tournaments. It is also
essential for recruiting new players to the game, allowing them to get
hooked on the fun after a minimal initial investment.

The playability factor discussed above, as it relates to rarity, is
present in all the sets. It is particularly prevalent in the Sabbat set,
which must juggle 10 different clans, 13 different disciplines, and 4
different titles, and provide cards specific to all of them. The result
is that almost every uncommon or rare has some sort of play requirement
that would make it very hard to constuct a deck from a limited set.
Fortunately, what you mostly get are commons, which have no extraordinary
play requirements.

Other cards are rare for obvious reasons that do not directly relate to
anything above. Take Praxis Siezures, for instance. These relate to the
uniqueness issue above, but even if their effects did not lead to
contestation one would hardly need for all 9 of these cards to be common.
While it is conceivable that one might need 18 Praxis Siezures for your
various decks, this would only come to 2 of each. One is hardly going to
need 20 copies of Praxis Siezure: Washington DC the way you might need 20
copies of Conservative Agitation for your various decks. It is only
proper that these cards should be rare.

Another need that is served by the traditional rarity scheme is that of
juggling card *variety* with the need for *multiple* cards in reasonably
focussed decks. Strategy in Jyhad depends on combos, and even in a
40-card deck, you cannot rely on pulling your planned combo unless you put
at least 3 or 4 or each needed card. There are about 430 cards total in
the original set. If all were of equal rarity, you would have to purchase
1200 to 1600 cards before you could count on having 3 or 4 an *any* cards
you needed to make a focussed deck. With the rarity scheme, however, you
do obtain multiples of the *common* cards after a much smaller total card
investment. The price paid, of course, is that the new player has a much
smaller *variety* of cards -- but at least he has *enough* of those cards
he has to make playable decks. WOTC expects, of course, that the new
player will eventually get bored of playing the same decks, and invest in
a greater card collection in pursuit of greater variety.

Which brings me to another aspect of Jyhad's rarity scheme: the tendency
for rare cards, within specific disciplines, to represent atypical
abilities within that discipline. Most of the disciplines in Jyhad seem
to have a basic focus that is well represented by the common cards. For
instance: Auspex has intercept; Obfuscate has stealth; Fortitude has
damage prevention; Potence inflicts increased damage; Celerity is best at
maneuvers, presses, and additional strikes; Dominate is great for
bleeding; and Presence for Voting and Combat avoidance. Once the new
player has gotten used to (and perhaps a bit bored by) these trends, he
may, by expanding his card collection, explore some more esoteric
possibilities of the discipline he chooses too play with. Thus we have
rare Obfuscate combat cards like Behind You; rare celerity bleed cards
like Cat Burglary; rare dominate cards like Far Mastery; rare Fortitude
crds like Freak Drive and Day Operation; Auspex vote cards like Telepathic
Vote Counting;

Another consideration in determining if cards are rare is ease of use.
Take Burst of Sunlight, for instance. While this card is certainly
*playable" by a newbie, he is likely, while playing it, to do as much
damage to himself as to his opponent. The card makes sense only as part
of some combo that includes damage prevention, or get out of torpor free
actions. You have to have the right cards in the right combinations to
play this card *effectively*, and you are likely to need to have a
considerable card collection before you can put together a reasonably
focussed deck. In the meantime, a new player woule do better putting the
much more common thaumaturgy cards, like Theft of Vitae, in his beginning
Tremere decks.

I could probably go on. The short of it is that the traditional rarity
scheme is a good idea for a whole host of reasons that you have neglected
to consider, and perhaps for a few more that I have not thought of either.
You clearly have not thought this through well enought o level any
sweeping criticisms.

I understand the reasons for your proposal: some people are penalized
(in a way) because they don't have access to the same cards (useful
rares, in particular) that other players do. That is inherent in CCGs.

But the solution (a 2CL on rares) doesn't really work well for several
reasons:

*) Not everyone even has 2 of every useful rare. Someone without *any*
Protected Resources or Tomb of Ramses (for examples) will not be
able to put 2 of those cards into her deck even if her deck would
benefit from them. Therefore her decks that would benefit from them
(by just a tiny, non-negligible bit) will be at a (tiny
non-negligible) disadvantage to other decks that a built by players
who _can_ put those cards into their decks.
A card limit (2CL on rares, 4CL in general, etc.) chooses an
arbitrary "spending level" - typically based on someone's personal
experience. If everyone has 10 of every rare, then a 10CL on rares
is adequate. If *any*one has *no* rares, then they would obviously
benefit from a 0CL (ban) on rares. This arbitrary sort of rule is
"Not a good thing".

*) A CL on rares is problematic for cards like Immortal Grapple which
are simultaneously rare and uncommon.

*) A CL on rares is a logistical nightmare for tournament judges who
have to go through each deck checking for violations.

Because this isn't _like_ trying to survive and thrive in real life,
that's why. If a large number of people are significantly disadvantaged
by the printing policy of a CCG manufacturer that makes the game subject
to money advantages, everyone suffers - not just the poor. As a
well-to-do player, all the IGs in the world are not going to find me a
challenging and clever opponent who makes the game fun to play.

What you're completely missing here is that the intellectual merits of
arguments about the benefits of avoiding the "good rares" problem in a
CCG are pretty much orthagonal to who's making them. Making cracks
about "deadbeat players whining about the world owing them rare cards"
may seem satisfying on an emotional level but they don't answer the
points the previous poster had been making. To answer those reasonably,
stick to what the majority are saying: that Jyhad is in fact a reasonbly
priced CCG influenced far more by skill and by the use of a relatively
large number of inexpensive commons and not by $10 and $20 rares.

>> A rich person will never whine about being owed 25 IGs
>
>...and neither will a person who works to buy the cards. My point is
>that those with more expendable money can buy more stuff. Period.
>That's life in a capitalistic society, and that's life in a CCG.

You're being overly simplistic. This could also be life in a CCG
where the manufacturer prints a couple dozen "win game" cards, the play
of which enables the bearer to immediately oust all of his opponents
and win the game. Such a card would be worth hundreds or thousands
of dollars and get purchased by rich people and those willing to work to
buy them. Or that is, they would if you could get people to play such a
ridiculous game whose outcome depended greatly on who owns what valuable
card. *That* is what the argument is really about: whether or not Jyhad
needs CL to avoid that kind of influence (and whether CL would actually
be much of a benifit in that sense). Your smug little tirade about
the CCG equivalent of welfare loafers whining that they can't afford the
cards just misses the point.

Fred
